name: Lhowa
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Regmi, Dan Raj & Ambika Regmi. 2024. Lhowa Phonology: A Typological Perspective. Gipan 6(1): 57-70. doi:10.3126/gipan.v6i1.68134
catalog_locator: pp.66-67 ('Syllable Structure' and 'Tones') and p.68 (end of 'Tone Melodies')
catalog_quote: [p.66] Lhowa is a tonal language. However, in Lhowa, morphemes or words are the domain of pitch contrasts. ... In Lhowa, like in Lhasa Tibetan (DeLancey, 2003, p.272) each syllable is intrinsically high or low. In Lhowa, tone (viz., pitch variation) is used to distinguish lexical meaning. Lhowa, like Lhasa Tibetan (DeLancey, 2003,p.272), exhibits a word tone system. The high vs. low tone is distinguished only on the first syllable of a word. Like Lamjung Yolmo (Gawne, 2016, p33), Lhowa presents a binary high/low lexical tone. [p.68] It is to be noted that like Tibetan, Lhowa is more a pitch-accent language than a true tone language. Lhowa contains word accents in which one syllable in a word or morpheme is more prominent than the others. However, the syllable in which accent is placed is indicated by a contrasting pitch (high vs. low tone). In English, the accentuated syllable is indicated by loudness.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Lhowa has a binary high/low word-tone (pitch accent-like) system: the tonal contrast is realized only on the first syllable of the word, and non-initial syllables of compounds take predictable melodies (HH, LH, LL, HL). Word prominence ('accent') is said to be marked by pitch rather than loudness; no independent loudness-stress position is stated, though the locus of the contrast is the word-initial syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds and certain derived/inflected verb forms show four tone melodies (HH, LH, LL, HL); no tone sandhi. Authors note an instrumental study is still needed.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/morpheme is the domain of pitch contrast; statements based on citation forms and compounds; impressionistic (no acoustic measurements).
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: Regmi & Regmi 2024 describe Lhowa/Loke of Upper Mustang (data from Lomanthang and Ghiling speakers) = lowa1242 proper (2021 census name 'Lhopa'). Nagano 1983/1985 describe the Lo Monthang variety (gLo-skad) from one emigre speaker. Kretschmar 1995 (list of works to obtain) describes the South/Lower Mustang (Baragaon) dialect, a distinct variety that Glottolog also files under lowa1242.

sources.note: Sociolinguistic survey with no tone analysis: wordlists mark a low tone (breathy diacritic under the vowel) against unmarked high on Loke forms, with a disclaimer that tone was not analysed.

tone.quote: Some language varieties bear distinct tonal differences, which have been analyzed to a lesser degree. Among these only the low tone is marked by using a diacritic for breathiness under the vowel of the syllable bearing the low tone. It should be noted that the wordlist data is from field transcription and has not undergone thorough phonological and grammatical analysis. … The breathy symbol on vowels is used to denote low tone, e.g., [ṳ]. High tone is not marked. … low vs. high tone (tone was not marked in all wordlists)
